prompt: Where is a V4 signed URL's signature computed?
hint: Think about what `sign.py` sent before it printed.

choices.text: On Cloud Storage, which records it in a list of issued links
choices.why: Nothing is recorded anywhere; the service only verifies a signature when the URL is used.

choices.text: On the signer's computer, from the private key
choices.why: Right. Making a URL sends no request, which is why a URL for a missing object was signed without complaint.

choices.text: On Google's IAM service, every time
choices.why: Only when signing by impersonation; with a key file it is purely local.

choices.text: In the browser of whoever opens the link
choices.why: The reader only presents the URL; it cannot sign anything.

prompt: A signed URL for an invoice is pasted into a supplier chat. What does anybody reading the chat learn?
hint: Look at the `X-Goog-Credential` parameter.

choices.text: The service account's private key
choices.why: The key never leaves the signer; only the signature does.

choices.text: Nothing, since the URL is encrypted
choices.why: Nothing in it is encrypted; the parameters are plain text.

choices.text: The signer, and a working link
choices.why: Right: they learn which service account signed it, and can download the invoice until it expires. The URL is the permission, and the signer's identity is written in it.

choices.text: The supplier's password
choices.why: A signed URL carries no password of anybody's.

prompt: What is the longest a V4 signed URL may be valid for, in seconds?
hint: The library refused 604,801.

prompt: In the lab, a URL valid for one second was used three seconds later and the report came back. What does that show about Cloud Storage?
hint: Who answered the request?

choices.text: Cloud Storage allows a grace period after expiry
choices.why: The request never reached Cloud Storage; the emulator answered it.

choices.text: Nothing about Cloud Storage
choices.why: Right: fake-gcs-server reads no signature, so the lab cannot test expiry. It also served a tampered URL and one with no signature at all.

choices.text: That `X-Goog-Expires` is counted in minutes
choices.why: It is in seconds, as `300` for five minutes showed.

choices.text: That the library rounds a short expiry up to a minute
choices.why: The URL said `X-Goog-Expires=1`; nothing rounded it.

prompt: A service account that signed hundreds of week-long URLs has its key leaked. What makes every URL it signed stop working?
hint: Cloud Storage checks the signer at the moment of use.

choices.text: Waiting seven days
choices.why: That works, but only after a week of exposure.

choices.text: Deleting the key
choices.why: Right, or removing the account's read permission. Each URL is verified against a key and a signer's permissions that no longer exist.

choices.text: Changing the object's storage class
choices.why: The class has nothing to do with who may read.

choices.text: Turning on public access prevention
choices.why: A signed URL is not public access, so prevention does not stop it.

prompt: Who is `allAuthenticatedUsers` in a Cloud Storage grant?
hint: Its name made it sound safe.

choices.text: Anybody signed in to any Google account
choices.why: Right: not Quitanda's users, everybody with a Google account.

choices.text: Every user of Quitanda's organisation
choices.why: That is what people assumed, and it is wrong.

choices.text: Service accounts of the same project
choices.why: Those are named one by one, or through a role on the project.

choices.text: Anybody on the internet, signed in or not
choices.why: That is `allUsers`.

prompt: What does uniform bucket-level access change on a bucket?
hint: Two permission systems, one switched off.

choices.text: It turns ACLs off
choices.why: Right: IAM is left as the only place access is granted, and it is needed for IAM conditions on the bucket.

choices.text: It makes every object public
choices.why: It grants nothing to anybody.

choices.text: It copies the bucket's ACL onto every object
choices.why: That was a way of working before it; uniform access ignores ACLs.

choices.text: It encrypts objects with one key
choices.why: Encryption is a different setting.

prompt: Against fake-gcs-server, `gcloud storage buckets get-iam-policy` on a bucket that exists answers `404`. Why?
hint: The emulator implements objects, not every API.

choices.text: The bucket name is wrong
choices.why: The bucket had just been created and listed.

choices.text: The emulator has no IAM
choices.why: Right: the request finds nothing to answer it. Nothing about IAM can be practised against it.

choices.text: The project has no owner
choices.why: gcloud sends no credentials here, and the emulator checks none.

choices.text: Uniform bucket-level access hides the policy
choices.why: Uniform access makes IAM the only system; it hides nothing.

prompt: In the lab, a `curl` with no credentials read a report that no grant had made public. What does a successful anonymous read from the emulator tell you about the same object on Cloud Storage?
hint: The emulator checks no credentials on any request.

choices.text: That it is public there too
choices.why: The emulator serves private objects to anybody, so its answer says nothing.

choices.text: That its ACL grants READER to allUsers
choices.why: The report had no such ACL; the emulator served it anyway.

choices.text: That public access prevention is off
choices.why: The emulator does not keep that setting, on or off.

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right. The only test of whether an object is public is an anonymous request to the real service.

prompt: A bucket already has `allUsers` granted `roles/storage.objectViewer`, and public access prevention is then set to `enforced`. What happens to the grant?
hint: Enforced does two things.

choices.text: Nothing, because prevention only refuses new grants
choices.why: It also makes existing public grants stop working.

choices.text: It stays in the policy and grants nothing
choices.why: Right, which is why switching prevention on closes a leak at once.

choices.text: It is deleted from the policy
choices.why: The grant stays written; it just has no effect.

choices.text: It is changed to `allAuthenticatedUsers`
choices.why: That would still be public; prevention neutralises both.

prompt: In Google Cloud CLI 591.0.0, which form sets public access prevention to `enforced` on a bucket?
hint: The form with `=enforced` was refused.

choices.text: `--public-access-prevention=enforced`
choices.why: This version refuses it: `ignored explicit argument 'enforced'`.

choices.text: `--pap=on`
choices.why: The flag takes no value at all.

choices.text: `--public-access-prevention` alone
choices.why: Right; `--no-public-access-prevention` sets `inherited`.

choices.text: `--uniform-bucket-level-access`
choices.why: That is a different setting, which turns ACLs off.

prompt: A bucket reports public access prevention `inherited`. Is it protected?
hint: Inherited from what?

choices.text: Yes, inherited always means enforced
choices.why: It means the bucket follows its organisation; there may be nothing to follow.

choices.text: No, inherited means off
choices.why: It can be protected, if a policy above enforces prevention.

choices.text: Only with a policy above it
choices.why: Right: an organisation policy that enforces the constraint, and the bucket alone cannot say whether one does.

choices.text: Only if it also has uniform access
choices.why: Uniform access turns ACLs off; it does not block grants to allUsers through IAM.

prompt: Match each organisation policy constraint to what it prevents.
hint: Two are about storage, two about IAM.

pairs.right: Access granted object by object through ACLs
A grant to a principal outside the organisation's domains

right_distractors: An object deleted before its retention period

prompt: Why is an organisation policy a stronger defence than setting public access prevention on each bucket?
hint: Think about next year's bucket.

choices.text: It is cheaper per bucket
choices.why: Neither has a price; the difference is who has to remember.

choices.text: It also encrypts the buckets
choices.why: Encryption is unrelated.

choices.text: It covers buckets not yet created
choices.why: Right, in projects nobody has heard of yet. A bucket setting protects that bucket; a constraint protects every bucket below it.

choices.text: It cannot be overridden anywhere below it
choices.why: It can be overridden on a folder or project, which is why overrides are reviewed first.

prompt: With `iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation` enforced, how does Quitanda still sign URLs for suppliers?
hint: There is a way to sign with no key file on any disk.

choices.text: It cannot sign URLs any more
choices.why: Signing by impersonation needs no downloaded key.

choices.text: With a key created before the constraint
choices.why: That key would still be a downloaded key, the thing the constraint is there to end.

choices.text: By making the invoices bucket public
choices.why: That is the leak this lesson is about.

choices.text: By impersonation, 12 hours at most
choices.why: Right: with `--impersonate-service-account`, Google's IAM credentials service signs, and no private key leaves Google.

prompt: A bucket was public for a month. Which record tells Quitanda who actually read the objects?
hint: Some logs are on only if somebody turned them on before.

choices.text: Admin Activity audit logs
choices.why: They record who changed the bucket's settings or IAM, not who read objects.

choices.text: Data Access or usage logs, if on before
choices.why: Right; and for public objects the documentation points to usage logs, since audit logs do not record those requests.

choices.text: Cloud Asset Inventory
choices.why: It shows what is open now, not who walked through.

choices.text: Security Command Center findings for the bucket
choices.why: A finding says a bucket is public, not who read it.

prompt: Order Quitanda's protections from the broadest net to the narrowest.
hint: The organisation first, the single URL last.
items: Public access prevention and uniform access on each bucket
IAM grants narrowed by a condition
Short signed URLs signed by impersonation

prompt: What is the one check of whether an object is public that the lesson says is worth trusting?
hint: It checks the result, not the settings.

choices.text: Reading the bucket's IAM policy
choices.why: It misses ACLs and settings above the bucket.

choices.text: An anonymous request from outside
choices.why: Right, expecting a refusal. Against the emulator it cannot fail, which is why it belongs to the real service.

choices.text: Listing the bucket with gcloud
choices.why: A listing made with your credentials says nothing about strangers.

choices.text: Checking that the bucket name is hard to guess
choices.why: A name is not a permission.

prompt: Match each way a bucket leaked to the protection that would have stopped it.
hint: One protection per shape.

pairs.left: A grant of objectViewer to allUsers on the bucket
A grant to allAuthenticatedUsers meant for colleagues
A service account key committed to a repository

prompt: A supplier needs one invoice today. Which is the narrowest way to give it?
hint: Narrow in time and in what it reaches.

choices.text: Grant the supplier's Google account objectViewer on the bucket
choices.why: That reaches every invoice, for as long as the grant lasts.

choices.text: A signed URL valid for minutes
choices.why: Right, for that object, signed by impersonation: one object, one request, a short life and no key file.

choices.text: Make the invoice public until the supplier confirms
choices.why: Public is anybody, and confirming is a step somebody forgets.

choices.text: A signed URL valid for seven days, to be safe
choices.why: Seven days is the longest allowed, and the longest a leaked link works.

prompt: The special principal that means anybody on the internet, signed in or not, is written `___` in an IAM binding or an ACL.
hint: Its sibling covers every signed-in Google account.
